Largo al factotum, Make way for the factotum, is the swaggering baritone aria sung by Figaro in Act I of Gioachino Rossini's opera The Barber of Seville. In this patter aria, Figaro introduces himself with boastful charm, cataloging his services as barber, surgeon, and man-of-all-trades while prancing about the town square. The aria showcases a baritone's ability to deliver rapid-fire lyrics with comic precision, and it stands as one of opera's most delightful and instantly memorable show-stoppers.

Rossini composed this for baritone voice. It is one of the most written-about arias in opera and a signature vehicle for baritone virtuosity. The title character Figaro is not merely a barber but the factotum, the man-of-all-work. He shaves, bleeds, and sets bones, and is intimate with every household and secret in Seville.

The aria is a patter aria, filled with rapid syllable-driven singing that requires comedic timing and clear diction. The orchestra accompanies with a bouncy, almost dance-like rhythm. Figaro's self-description, "Figaro qua, Figaro là, Figaro su, Figaro giù," is the aria's most famous refrain, establishing his ubiquitous, indispensable presence.

The aria's opening phrase "Largo al factotum" is an instruction to the crowd to make way for the factotum, reinforcing Figaro's importance and cheeky self-regard. Rossini's witty orchestration, particularly the use of pizzicato strings and lighthearted woodwinds, underscores the aria's comedic spirit and operatic farce. This aria is considered essential repertoire for any baritone and appears frequently at concert galas and auditions, often bringing down the house with its infectious energy.
